questions.question: A data-response graph shows a monopolist with demand labelled AR, marginal revenue below it, average cost of R125 and price of R150 at the equilibrium output of 100 units. Work through the full marking chain: the equilibrium rule, the readings, the profit calculation, and the reason marginal revenue sits below demand.
questions.expected_answer: Equilibrium rule first: the monopolist produces where marginal cost equals marginal revenue. Reading the graph: the equilibrium quantity of 100 units sits below that intersection; the selling price of R150 is read UP from that quantity to the demand (AR) curve; the average cost of R125 is read from the average cost curve at the same quantity. Calculation as number sentences: profit per unit = price − average cost = R150 − R125 = R25; total economic profit = R25 × 100 = R2 500 — method line, subtraction, multiplication and a labelled answer each carry marks, and 'show all calculations' means writing every step. Marginal revenue lies below the demand curve because the monopolist must lower the price on ALL units to sell an additional one, so the extra revenue from the last unit is less than its price. The profit is ECONOMIC profit — earnings above normal profit, which is already included in average cost as the reward for entrepreneurship — and it can persist in the long run because barriers to entry prevent rivals from competing it away; were average cost above price, the identical procedure would deliver the economic loss.

questions.question: From the practice table — CPI of 120,0 last year and 127,2 this year; basket weights food 40% up 8%, transport 35% up 6%, education 25% up 4% — calculate the inflation rate and the weighted increase, name the classic error in each, and classify the inflation if fuel and electricity led the increases.
questions.expected_answer: Inflation rate = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (127,2 − 120,0) ÷ 120,0 × 100 = 7,2 ÷ 120,0 × 100 = 6,0%. The classic error is dividing by the new index — the rate measures growth from the starting point, so the OLD index is the denominator; a second trap is reporting the 7,2-point change as 7,2%. Weighted increase = 0,4 × 8 + 0,35 × 6 + 0,25 × 4 = 3,2 + 2,1 + 1,0 = 6,3%. The classic error is averaging the three increases without weights, which ignores that food's heavy share drags the average toward food's experience — also the reason low-income households, whose real baskets are food-heavy, live harsher inflation than the headline number. If fuel and electricity led the increases, the inflation is cost-push: costs entering from the supply side rather than excess spending. The policy consequence completes the higher-order answer: raising the repo rate cools borrowing and spending but cannot cheapen fuel or tariffs, so monetary tightening against cost-push inflation buys little disinflation at a high cost in output and jobs, and fiscal discipline over administered prices attacks the engine more directly.

questions.question: Plan the forty-mark essay 'Compare and contrast perfect competition and monopoly in detail, and use a graph to explain the monopoly's long-run equilibrium', naming the mark allocation of each part and the content that fills it.
questions.expected_answer: Introduction (max 2): define a market structure as the way a market is organised — the number of sellers, nature of the product and ease of entry — without borrowing the question's wording. Main body (max 26): paired contrasts at two marks per developed pair — number of firms (very many vs one); product (homogeneous vs unique without close substitutes); entry (free vs blocked by natural cost advantages, licences, patents); price control (price taker vs price maker still bound by demand); information (perfect vs restricted); demand curve (horizontal for the individual competitor vs downward-sloping with marginal revenue below it); long-run profit (normal only, as entry competes gains away, vs persistent economic profit behind barriers); efficiency (productive and allocative efficiency vs lower output at higher price); examples (fresh produce markets vs a sole utility). The graph, described verbally: long-run equilibrium output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, price above on the demand curve, and the economic-profit rectangle between price and average cost across the equilibrium quantity, persisting because entry is blocked. Additional part (max 10): own judgement — economies of scale can justify regulated natural monopolies, but unregulated dominance transfers welfare from consumers and dulls innovation, which is why the Competition Commission, Tribunal and Appeal Court police abuse; anchor with South African cases such as prosecuted cartels. Conclusion (max 2): one fresh judgement, for example that structure shapes conduct, so policy watches structure. Total 40.
